extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, philosophy, social science, and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Establishing a deductive science (Ethology) that explains how character is formed from general psychological laws and particular circumstances, and prescribing methodological principles for doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an Empirical Law
rubrics_metrics.description: An Empirical Law is "a uniformity, whether of succession or of co-existence, which holds true in all instances within our limits of observation, but is not of a nature to afford any assurance that it would hold beyond those limits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirical laws as observed generalizations that require explanation; do not assume they are ultimate or universally valid without analyzing their causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand to resolve empirical laws into causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws are not ultimate laws of nature but consequences of causal laws; the really scientific truths are the causal laws which explain empirical generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting an empirical regularity, a robust account must identify the underlying causal laws and specify the conditions under which the empirical law holds; otherwise limit claims to verification rather than explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit applicability of empirical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws are "approximate generalizations" that depend on particular conditions: they may hold within observed limits but fail when time, place, or circumstances differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overgeneralizing observed maxims (e.g., national or age stereotypes); explicitly state contextual limits and test whether the causal conditions extend to new cases before applying the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Deductive Method for complex human phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: For complex facts like the formation of character, the Deductive Method, "setting out from general laws, and verifying their consequences by specific experience," is alone applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure inquiry by deducing consequences from general psychological laws and then seek empirical verification, rather than attempting fully controlled experiments on whole complex human lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethology as a deductive science of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethology (science of the formation of character) is defined as the science that "determines the kind of character produced in conformity to [general laws] by any set of circumstances, physical and moral."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing theory about character formation, deduce particular tendencies from general psychological laws given assumed circumstances and report conclusions as tendencies, not certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific propositions about character must assert tendencies, not certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions in Ethology "must not assert that something will always, or certainly, happen; but only that such and such will be the effect of a given cause, so far as it operates uncounteracted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase claims about character and social effects in terms of tendencies and conditional effects (e.g., 'tends to', 'is likely to'), and explicitly acknowledge possible counteracting influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical impossibility of fully controlled experiments on character formation
rubrics_metrics.description: To perform proper experiments on character formation one would need to know and record "every sensation or impression received by the young pupil" from infancy, which is impossible; trivial unnoticed circumstances can vitiate such experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and document the limits of experimental claims about upbringing/education; avoid asserting causal claims based on insufficiently controlled or under-observed interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of simple observation and the need for large, comparable samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational inferences about character must be made "en masse"; conclusions deserve no reliance unless instances are sufficiently numerous to eliminate chance and shared circumstantial confounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sufficiently large, representative samples and comparative designs (ratios/degrees across groups) when inferring general tendencies from observation; be cautious about claims based on small or anecdotal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of analyzing simple component causes first
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the laws of the simple causes of complex phenomena first, then deduce how their composition produces complex effects (the science should "try its experiments not on the complex facts, but on the simple ones of which they are compounded").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose complex psychological phenomena into simpler mechanisms and test these where possible before assembling them into explanations of character-level outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and priority of middle principles (axiomata media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle principles (axiomata media) are the most valuable part of a science; they are the intermediate laws that link general laws to empirical phenomena, and need not always be derived only by induction from lower facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing theory, aim to identify and justify middle-level principles, and be open to deriving them deductively from higher laws provided they are subsequently verified against empirical generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification: compare deductions to empirical generalizations, not single instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying deductive explanations we should verify deductions by comparing them with general propositions drawn from many instances (empirical laws), rather than matching them to single occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregate empirical regularities (not isolated cases) to test and refine deductive theories; successful deduction should reproduce known empirical generalizations (e.g., derive Kepler's laws rather than every individual planetary position).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for multiple classes of causes shaping mental differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of mind may be (1) original facts, (2) consequences of previous mental history, or (3) depend on varieties of physical organization; often mixtures of these operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In explanatory accounts, enumerate and evaluate contributions from innate predispositions, developmental/educational history, and organic/physiological factors rather than attributing differences to a single source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider mediation of organic differences through sensations and mental laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Organic differences in bodily organization may affect mental phenomena indirectly by altering sensation intensity/quality, which then, by "mere mental laws," produces different higher mental states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should trace whether physiological differences act directly on higher mental functions or operate via changed sensory experiences and associative processes; avoid simplistic one-step biological attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against mistaking persistent empirical observances for immutable nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The text warns that many prefer to treat observed mental differences as "ultimate facts, incapable of being either explained or altered" rather than seeking causal explanations; this is to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques and theories should challenge assumptions that observed regularities are immutable; propose and test hypotheses about how changing circumstances or education might modify observed characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge scientific incompleteness and revise with advances (e.g., cerebral physiology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of cerebral and nervous physiology is rapidly advancing and may change our understanding of connections between organic structure and mental phenomena; prior doctrines like phrenology are untenable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain openness to revising theoretical accounts in light of new physiological evidence; explicitly separate well-supported claims from speculative ones and update explanations as relevant empirical knowledge progresses.
